what-the-cloud-is.title: Welcome to What the cloud actually is, part of Cloud Computing & DevOps.
what-the-cloud-is.idea: Every organisation in Ghana that runs software now faces the same decision: a server in a room with a UPS, or a cloud account billed monthly. The honest answer is usually "both, for different things" — and the reason to understand the cloud properly is that the wrong choice is expensive in a way that is hard to reverse. Migration is cheap in one direction (a test database) and painful in the other (three years of accumulated configuration nobody documented).
what-the-cloud-is.example: Take one small web application with a database and about 5,000 daily users, and price the three approaches honestly by work, not just money. A server in the office. A tower machine, a UPS, a fixed IP from the ISP, and somebody on call when the power or disk fails. Monthly cost is low and known; risk sits entirely with you, and scaling means buying hardware. This is still the right answer for some workloads — a lab machine, an internal tool with no public exposure — and it is a good place to learn Linux. IaaS. Two virtual machines across two zones behind a load balancer, a managed database with automated backups, object storage for uploads. You patch the operating system, harden SSH, manage certificates and write the deployment scripts. You get real availability and an hourly bill. PaaS plus managed services. Push a container or a repository; the platform builds, runs, scales and issues TLS certificates. The database is a managed connection string. You now spend your time on the application and the data model. The trade-off is less control (you cannot tune the kernel) and vendor-specific behaviours you must learn. The lesson is that the decision is not "cloud or not". It is which layer of responsibility you want to own for each part of your system — and it is normal to answer differently for different components.
what-the-cloud-is.challenge: Write a two-page decision note for an organisation choosing where to host a customer-facing service: the workload and its peak-to-average ratio, three options (on-premises, IaaS, managed platform) with monthly cost and operational effort estimated, the data-protection constraint, the failure modes of each, and a recommendation with the reasoning that a non-technical director could follow and challenge.

cloud-native-architecture.title: Welcome to Cloud-native architecture, part of Cloud Computing & DevOps.
cloud-native-architecture.idea: A server that has been running in a cupboard for three years is designed around the assumption that it will keep running. The cloud breaks that assumption deliberately: instances are replaced, zones fail, capacity moves. Software that was written for the cupboard behaves badly in the cloud — losing sessions when it scales, storing uploads on a disk that vanishes with the instance, and failing entirely when a dependency slows down.
cloud-native-architecture.example: An application keeps logins in memory, stores uploads on the instance disk, and calls a payment API synchronously with no timeout. On one server it works for years. Behind a load balancer with two instances, users are logged out at random and half the avatars are broken, and when the payment provider slows down the whole site waits. The repair is four changes, none of them exotic: 1. Move sessions to a shared store. A Redis instance (or a signed cookie if the session is small) means any instance can serve any request. 2. Move uploads to object storage. The instance becomes disposable; images are served through a CDN. 3. Put the payment call behind a queue. The request returns "payment pending" immediately; a worker processes it with retries and the UI polls status. Slow providers now cost latency in one feature, not availability of the site. 4. Add timeouts, retries and a circuit breaker on every outbound call, and health/readiness endpoints so the platform replaces a sick instance instead of routing traffic into it. Read the Terraform below as the shape of the change: stateless compute, managed state, a queue in the middle, and a bucket for files.
cloud-native-architecture.challenge: Produce an architecture diagram and a one-page rationale for a service that must survive the loss of one availability zone, a surge of five times normal traffic for an hour, and a slow third-party API — while staying inside a stated monthly budget. Label every managed service, state the maximum instance count, and list the three failure modes you accept rather than solve.

containers-and-infrastructure-as-code.title: Welcome to Containers and infrastructure as code, part of Cloud Computing & DevOps.
containers-and-infrastructure-as-code.idea: Two teams describe the same outage. One says "it worked in staging", because staging had Python 3.11 and production had 3.9. The other says "the security group was fine", because somebody changed it in the console in February and nobody wrote it down. Containers and infrastructure as code exist to remove both sentences from your vocabulary, and together they are the difference between environments that can be recreated and environments that can only be feared.
containers-and-infrastructure-as-code.example: The Dockerfile below builds a Node.js API: dependencies installed first, a non-root user, one process per container, and a start command that is the only thing that varies between environments — everything else comes from the environment. The Terraform that follows describes the same application in a cloud account: a network, two app instances behind a load balancer, and a managed database in a separate private subnet that nothing on the internet can reach. Nothing here is clicked in a console, so the whole environment can be created in a second region, reviewed by a colleague, and destroyed without leftovers. Read them together and the division of responsibility is clear: the image says what the application is; the infrastructure says where it runs and what it may talk to.
containers-and-infrastructure-as-code.challenge: Deliver one application as a container plus infrastructure as code: a pinned, multi-stage Dockerfile running as non-root, a compose file for local development, and Terraform that creates a network, two app instances, an autoscaling maximum and a private managed database. Deploy it, destroy it, redeploy it in under thirty minutes, and write the commands into a README that a colleague can run without asking you anything.

ci-cd-observability-and-incidents.title: Welcome to CI/CD, observability and incident response, part of Cloud Computing & DevOps.
ci-cd-observability-and-incidents.idea: The goal of this lesson is boring deployments. A team that can ship ten times a day and roll back in two minutes has an enormous advantage over one that ships monthly and holds its breath: smaller changes, faster feedback, less pressure to be perfect. Getting there needs a pipeline, a release strategy, and enough visibility to know when something is wrong — before a customer tells you.
ci-cd-observability-and-incidents.example: The pipeline below is deliberately ordinary. The interesting part is what happened after it deployed: a canary caught a regression that unit tests could not, because the bug was in a query plan rather than in logic. Read the sequence as a narrative. The canary is at 5%; the error rate for the new version is 3.1% against a baseline of 0.4%; the alert fires on the SLO rather than on a CPU threshold; and because the artifact was tagged and the previous version is still running in the other half of the fleet, the rollback is a single re-point of the traffic rule. Total exposure: eleven minutes and about 200 users. Then the post-incident habit: a blameless review written within 48 hours, with a timeline, the contributing causes, and two action items — a missing index and an alert that arrives before the canary threshold does. No individual is named, because the goal is a better system, not a culpable person.
ci-cd-observability-and-incidents.challenge: Take one service from commit to production with a real pipeline: tests running on every push, one immutable artifact, a canary deploy with automatic rollback on error-rate regression, structured logs, latency percentiles and one SLO with an alert. Then deliberately introduce a subtle bug behind a feature flag, watch the canary and the alert catch it, roll back, and write the incident review with the two actions that would have caught it earlier.
